newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: IPC sees 60 pct profits from telecoms.
newsitem.headline: IPC sees 60 pct profits from telecoms.

text.p: Singapore's computer maker IPC Corp expects 60 percent of its group net profits to come from its telecommunications business this year, the Business Times newspaper said on Tuesday.
It quoted IPC chairman Patrick Ngiam as saying in Hanover the company intended to make Germany's Hagenuk Telecom GmbH into a subsidiary in the next few weeks.

Ngiam said at a technology fair in the German city telecommunications would supply 60 percent of ITC's net profits this year and the proportion would rise, possibly up to 80 percent in the next few years.
"We have decided to be a niche player in the computer world, and we are putting major efforts in telecommunications," Ngiam was quoted as saying.
IPC has a 37.5 percent stake in Hagenuk and planned to raise that to more than 50 percent in the next few weeks, Ngiam said.
IPC would subscribe to new shares to be issued by Hagenuk and was also discussing the purchase of some shares from Hagenuk's existing shareholders, the Business Times said.
IPC has invested Singapore S$50 million in Hagenuk through cash and a S$33 million issue of new IPC shares.
For the year ending March 31, 1998, Hagenuk's sales are projected at 760 million marks compared to 1996's 380 million marks.
Once Hagenuk became IPC's subsidiary, Ngiam said he expected telecommunications to account for up to half of the group's turnover this year.
The newspaper quoted him as saying Hagenuk should become a major telecommunications player with a 10 to 20 percent global market share in the next two to three years.
He said IPC was transforming itself because of changes and increasing competition in the market place.

For the fiscal year ended December 31, 1996, IPC reported net operating profit of S$13.5 million and suffered an extraordinary loss of S$37.43 million, due mostly to write-offs for its financially troubled South Korean unit and disposal of unprofitable overseas units.
The Business Times also quoted Ngiam as saying IPC must look again at its funding policy in the wake of a series of setbacks.

"I think we should adopt a more moderate borrowing policy and we should tap into the equity market to finance our growth. Because of the highly volatile nature of our business, most of our assets are intangible," he said.
Banks had extended some S$180 million in loans to IPC, he said.
